topic: Why traffic jams appear out of nowhere
core_explanation: In dense enough traffic, smooth flow is unstable: a small speed fluctuation is amplified as each following driver reacts with a delay and brakes a little harder. The disturbance grows into a stop-and-go wave (a 'phantom' jam) that travels backwards, against the direction of traffic, even with no accident or bottleneck.

claims.text: In a 2008 study, Japanese researchers put 22 cars on a 230 m circular track and asked drivers to cruise at about 30 km/h.
claims.notes: Paper: 'The drivers were requested to cruise at about 30 km/h'; authors at Nagoya University and other Japanese institutions.

claims.text: Even with no bottleneck, the uniform flow broke down and a jam emerged from small fluctuations.
claims.notes: Paper abstract: 'even a tiny fluctuation grows larger and then the homogeneous movement cannot be maintained'.

claims.text: The stop-and-go jam travels backwards, against the direction of traffic.
Small disturbances are amplified because following drivers react with a delay and brake harder than the car ahead (string instability).
claims.notes: Described as the instability of homogeneous flow; our 'brakes a little harder' wording is the standard intuitive description of amplification.

claims.text: On real highways, such jams typically drift backwards at roughly 15-20 km/h.
claims.notes: S1: ~20 km/h; S4: -15 +/- 5 km/h; S5: about -14.5 to -17 km/h. Use the range, not a single number.

claims.text: Field experiments later showed that controlling the speed of a single (automated) vehicle can dampen these waves.
claims.notes: Stern et al. 2018; single primary peer-reviewed source is acceptable for this narrow claim. The car was automated - say 'smoothly driven', not 'a human driver'.

claims.text: Leaving extra space and driving smoothly may help absorb such waves.
claims.notes: Inference from C6 applied to human drivers; must be phrased as 'might/could', never as a guarantee.

sources.title: Traffic jams without bottlenecks - experimental evidence for the physical mechanism of the formation of a jam
sources.publisher: New Journal of Physics (IOP / DPG), open access via University of Osaka
sources.key_excerpt: 22 vehicles, 230 m circuit, ~30 km/h; tiny fluctuations grow; jam cluster propagates backward at roughly 20 km/h, the common value measured on real highways.

sources.key_excerpt: Ring experiments with >20 vehicles: waves emerge consistently and can be dampened by controlling the velocity of a single vehicle.

sources.title: Empirical Features of Congested Traffic States and Their Implications for Traffic Modeling (Schoenhof & Helbing)
sources.key_excerpt: Stop-and-go waves propagate upstream at about -15 +/- 5 km/h.

sources.title: Common Traffic Congestion Features studied in USA, UK, and Germany (Kerner et al.)
sources.key_excerpt: Wide moving jam downstream fronts move upstream at roughly -14.5 to -17 km/h on freeways in three countries.

sources.title: Shockwave Traffic Jams Recreated For First Time

uncertainties: Jams only self-organise above a critical density; at low density small fluctuations die out.
Exact backward speeds vary by road and dataset (some studies report lower values).
The single-vehicle damping result comes from automated vehicles in controlled ring experiments; real multi-lane highways are more complex.
misleading_simplifications: Saying any single brake tap inevitably causes a massive jam.
Saying the jam moves forward with the cars.
Presenting simulation visuals as footage of the real experiment.
Implying one considerate human driver is guaranteed to fix a jam.
safe_analogies: A wave in a stadium crowd: people stay in place while the wave travels around the stands.
